Lignin dissolution and lignocellulose pretreatment by carboxylic acid based deep eutectic solvents

ª Beijing Key Laboratory of Lignocellulosic Chemistry, College of Materials Science and Technology, Beijing Forestry University, Beijing 100083, China b Department of Chemistry, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China
## ARTICLE INFO --- **Keywords:** Deep eutectic solvents Kraft lignin Lactic acid Pretreatment Kamlet-Taft parameters

ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) composed by carboxylic acids and quaternary ammonium salts are potential candidate for lignocellulose dissolution and pretreatment. To both explore the most efficient DESs for ligno-cellulose dissolution and pretreatment as well as unveil the process mechanism, DESs composed by carboxylic acids as the hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and quaternary ammonium salts as the hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) were prepared and further applied for kraft lignin (KL) dissolution as well as poplar and pine pretreat-ment. We found DES composed by lactic acid (LA) and allyltrimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC) with mole ratio of 2:1 is high-efficient for the dissolution of KL. In addition, 70% poplar lignin and 82% pine lignin could be removed at 120 °C for 6 h with a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:10. Furthermore, the -OH and -COOH groups in HBDs = of DESs provided active protons to cleave ether bonds and part of carbon-carbon bonds during lignin disso-lution and extraction. Additionally, the KL solubility and the Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters (a and π * ) of the DESs showed good positive correlation. These findings give a deep insight into the dissolution mechanism of KL and pretreatment of lignocellulose, which is helpful for designing robust DESs for dissolution and pretreatment of lignocellulose.

1. Introduction Lignin is the most abundant aromatic biopolymer in nature. Meanwhile, it is a sustainable precursor for producing aromatic chemicals. In the past decades, transformation of lignin into functional materials and value-added chemicals has drawn numerous attentions. Generally, dissolution is a prerequisite for effectively utilization/conversion of lignin (Chen et al., 2020b; Ragauskas Arthur et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017a, 2017b). However, lignin is composed by the cross link of three phenylpropane structure units through diverse linkages, which makes the dissolution of lignin highly difficult (Hong et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017).

Until now, several types of solvent systems have been applied in the dissolution of lignin, for example, ionic liquids (ILs), (An et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2019b; Rashid et al., 2016) mixture of ILs and water, (Xu et al., 2017) mixture of water and organic solvents (Zhang et al., 2017a, 2017b) or γ-valerolactone (Xue et al., 2016), and liquid ammonia (Strassberger et al., 2015). Although these solvent systems could dissolve lignin, they have some obvious drawbacks. Organic solvents are volatile, while liquid ammonia requires high pressure and low

temperature (Strassberger et al., 2015). ILs are usually expensive and viscous (Cao et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017a, 2017b). It is still a chal- lenge for designing novel and robust solvent systems to dissolve lignin.

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are cheap, easy to prepare, and can be designed to be non-toxic, biocompatible and biodegradable (Abbott et al., 2004, 2003; Paiva et al., 2014; van Osch et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2021). Recently, applications of DESs in pretreatment of lignocellulose have gained significant attention (Francisco et al., 2012; Lou and Zhang, 2022; Wang and Lee, 2021; Xu et al., 2021). Reports have shown that organic acids based DESs are highly efficient for lignocellulose pretreatment (Tan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Fran- cisco et al., 2012). For example, Alvarez-Vasco et al. used DESs composed by organic carboxylic acid (i.e., acetic acid, levulinic acid, and lactic acid (LA)) and choline chloride for delignification of hardwood and softwoods, and LA based DES showed the highest lignin extraction yields (78.5% from hardwoods and 58.2% from softwoods) (Alvar- ez-Vasco et al., 2016). Lynam et al. found that LA-based DESs could dissolve alkali lignin with the highest solubility of 13 wt% (Lynam et al., 2017). Hong et al. reported that LA and choline chloride-based DES is more efficient on separating alkali lignin from poplar than oxalic acid

and choline chloride-based DES (Hong et al., 2020a). Liang et al. used LA-based DESs for pretreatment of corn stover and found that both alkyl chain length and functional groups of HBAs significantly influence the efficiency of pretreatment (Liang et al., 2021). These discussions indi- cated that carboxylic-based DESs (especially LA) are efficient for lignocellulose pretreatment and dissolution because of the unique mo- lecular structure of LA, in which there are simultaneously one carboxyl group and one hydroxyl group. However, the solubility of lignin in the currently developed LA-based DESs was not satisfactory, and the mechanism of the better performance of LA-based DESs has not been well unveiled.

To enhance the solubility of lignin in LA-based DESs and reveal the enhancing effect of LA on lignin dissolution, herein, several carboxylic acids (i.e., LA, malic acid (MA) and glycolic acid (GA)) and quaternary ammonium salts (allyltrimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC), choline chloride (ChCl), tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC), and tetrae- thylammonium chloride (TEAC)) based DESs were prepared (Fig. S1). The solubility of kraft lignin (KL) in these DESs at 50 °C, 60 °C and 70 °C were measured. The relationship between lignin solubility and the Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters of the DESs was analyzed. The structural changes between the original and the regenerated lignin were charac- terized. In addition, pretreatment of poplar and pine with the designed DESs was conducted and the enhanced effect of the LA-based DESs on KL dissolution and lignocellulose pretreatment was investigated.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Kraft lignin (KL, with low sulfonate content) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Poplar (5 years old) wood was obtained from Hebei Province and pine (Pinus yunnanensis, 6 years old) wood was obtained from Yunnan Province. Choline chloride (ChCl), lactic acid (LA), allyl-trimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC), and glycolic acid (GA) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Malic acid (MA) and tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC) were bought from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd (Beijing, China). Tetraethylammonium chloride (TEAC) was purchased from Energy Chemical (Beijing, China).

## 2.2. Preparation of DESs The DESs were prepared by mixing the HBDs and HBAs at a molar ratio of 1:1 or 2:1 in a glass vial. Subsequently, the mixture was heated to 70 °C with a mechanical stirrer at 500 rpm until a transparent liquid was obtained. Finally, all DESs were stored under vacuum at 60 °C for 24 h to remove the contaminated trace water.

2.3. Determination of KL solubility in the prepared DESs The solubility of KL was measured based on our previously reported route (Yu et al., 2020). The KL solubility measurement consisted of a total of two steps. The first step was roughly measured, and 30 mg of KL was added to ca.1 g DES each time, and the addition is repeated until the added KL could not be completely dissolved within 1 h. The second step was accurately measured. 90% amount of the first-step achieved KL solubility was added to ca.1 g DES, then 3 mg of KL was added to DES each time until the KL could not be dissolved in 1 h. The detailed information was presented in Supplementary Information section.

2.4. *Pretreatment with DESs and composition analysis* The poplar and pine particles of sizes between 40 and 60 mesh were obtained by smash and then sieve the poplar and pine sample. After that, the wood powder was extracted with toluene–ethanol (2:1, v/v) in a Soxhlet instrument for 6 h. The poplar/pine powder were mixed with

LA-ATMAC-2:1 or LA-ChCl-2:1 with a mass ratio of 1:10 and put in an oil bath at 120 °C for 6 h, and followed by dilution with ethanol. The solid components were further separated and washed with ethanol and deionized water until the filtrate clarifies, and then freeze-dried for the followed analysis. The detailed pretreatment process was given in Supplementary Information section. The chemical compositions of poplar sample and the solid substrates were determined according to a reported procedure (Sluiter et al., 2010). The content of acid-insoluble lignin (AIL, Klason lignin) was determined by measuring the weight of the residue after drying. The absorbance of acid-soluble lignin (ASL) at 240 nm was determined by UV2310-vis spectrophotometer. The deter- mination of monomeric sugars in the aqueous soluble fraction per- formed on HPAEC system (Dionex ICS 3000, USA) equipped with a Carbopac TM PA-20 column (3 mm × 150 mm, Dionex, Sunnyvale, USA) and an amperometric detector. The details could be seen in Supple- mentary Information section too.

## 2.5. Structural characterization of KL Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were performed on a Bruker Avance 400 MHz spectrometer. The weight-average (M_w) and number-average (M_n) molecular weights of the two acetylated KL samples were analyzed by Gel Permeation Chromatography (GPC, Agilent 1200). Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) analysis was conducted on a Hitachi S-4800 Scanning Electron Microscope operated at 15 kV. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) experiment was conducted on a TGA Q500 (TA Instrument Company, America). Fourier Transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra were recorded on a Prestige-21 FT-IR Spectroscopy (Shimadzu, Japan). Detailed information was given in Supplementary Information section.

3. Results and discussion 3.1. Dissolution of KL in DESs The prepared DESs (Table S1) were denoted as HBD-HBA-x, where x represents the molar ratio of HBD and HBA. In Table S1, LA-TMAC-1:1 and GA-TMAC-1:1 could not form DESs. Subsequently, the prepared DESs were applied to dissolve KL at different temperatures (Fig. 1). Fig. 1 shows that the solubility of KL in all examined DESs increases with the dissolution temperature. When the molar ratio of HBD and HBA was 1:1, at 50 °C, LA-ATMAC-1:1 and LA-ChCl-1:1 could dissolve KL, but the solubility of KL in LA-TEMC-1:1 is less than 1 wt%. As shown in Fig. 1, LA-ATMAC-1:1 provides the best lignin solubility of 15.6 wt% at 70 °C, while the lignin solubility is only 2.9 wt% in LA-TEMC-1:1 at 70 °C. Fig. 1B shows that the solubility of KL is significantly enhanced to 22.5 wt% when the molar ratio of HBD and HBA increase to 2:1 for LA-ATMAC-2:1 at 70 °C. Notably, the solubility of KL at 70 °C increases with the following order: LA-TEAC-2:1 < LA-TMAC-2:1 < LA-ChCl-2:1 < LA-ATMAC-2:1. For the GA-based DESs, a similar tendency was observed (Fig. 1C and D). The GA-ATMAC-x showed the best performance at the same GA/HBA molar ratio, and high molar ratio of GA and HBAs is beneficial for the dissolution of KL. Meanwhile, the solubility of KL at 70 °C increases with the following order: GA-TEAC-2:1 < GA-TMAC-2:1 < GA-ChCl-2:1 < GA-ATMAC-2:1. GA-ATMAC-2:1 shows the maximum KL solubility of 19.1 wt% at 70 °C among all GA-based DESs (Fig. 1). Table S2 indicates that all the prepared MA-based DESs show poor performance on the KL dissolution even at 70 °C. From the above results, the functional groups in the employed HBAs significantly affect the KL dissolution, which followed the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl, and meanwhile, the KL solubility decreases with the increase of the cation size in HBAs, e.g., LA-TEAC-2:1 < LA-TMAC-2:1 and GA-TEAC-2:1 < GA-TMAC-2:1.

From the chemical structure of the used HBDs (LA, MA, and GA), the main difference of the used HBDs lies in that there are two -COOH groups in MA, while only one -COOH group in both LA and GA. Meanwhile, all the three HBDs contain one -OH group. The -OH group and -COOH groups in the HBD are beneficial for lignin dissolution, but more than one -COOH groups weaken the lignin dissolution (Tan et al., 2019). Consistent with Francisco's results (Francisco et al., 2012), MA-based DESs show poor KL dissolution ability. The presence of two -COOH groups in MA increases the number of hydrogen bonds and extensive dimer chains, which significantly increase the viscosity (Table S3) and thus decrease mass transfer and KL dissolution. In comparison, GA- and LA-based DESs perform similarly on KL dissolution, and the solubility of KL in these two types of DESs vary with the type of HBA and the HBD/HBA molar ratio. For example, the lignin solubility in LA-TMAC-2:1 is higher than that in GA-TMAC-2:1, while GA-TEAC-2:1 shows higher solubility than LA-TEAC-2:1. Moreover, LA-ChCl-1:1 shows higher KL solubility than GA-ChCl-1:1, but the solubility of KL in LA-ChCl-2:1 is lower than that in GA-ChCl-2:1. The different performance of the prepared LA- and GA-based DESs to dissolve KL will be discussed in the following section.

3.2. The effect of DESs' K-T parameters on KL dissolution K-T empirical parameters (i.e., α, β, and π *) of the solvents could be employed to evaluate the ability of the solvents to dissolve lignocellu-lose components. These parameters can be applied to quantify hydrogen-bond donating ability (acidity, α), hydrogen-bond accepting ability (basicity, β) and the polarizability (π*) of the solvents. The K-T empirical parameters of the prepared LA- and GA-based DESs were determined and given in Table S4. The correlation between KL solubil-ities (Fig. 1) and the K-T parameters Table S4 is very poor if all the LA-and GA-based DESs are considered. However, after carefully analyzing the obtained results, some regularities could still be observed. First, the solubilities of KL in LA- and GA-based DESs are similar

when they have the same HBA and molar ratio of HBD/HBA (Fig. 1). Correspondingly, K-T empirical parameters of LA- and GA-based DESS with same HBA and molar ratio of HBD/HBA are similar (Table S4) although the correlation between KL solubility and the K-T parameters is not completely consistent.

Second, compared with other HBAs, the alkyl chain of TEMC is longer and its volume is larger than that of the other three HBAs, which leads to its larger steric hindrance, causing the HBDs has a weak ability to form H-bonds with it (Zhou et al., 2022). In addition, the molar ratio of HBAs and HBDs also affects the dissolution ability of lignin. When the molar ratio of HBDs increased, LA and GA could provide more active protons, which promoted the dissolution of lignin (Zhou et al., 2022). As a result, LA-TEAC-1:1 and GA-TEAC-1:1 show the lowest values of α and π*, indicating that they have the poorest hydrogen-bond donating ability and lowest polarity. In contrast, the solvents possessing stronger hydrogen-bond donating ability and higher polarity have better ability to dissolve lignin (Liu et al., 2019a). Thereby, the solubility of KL in LA-TEAC-1:1 and GA-TEAC-1:1 is very low.

Third, the correlation between KL solubility in LA- and GA-based DESs and the K-T parameters was further analyzed by the statistical method of linear solvation energy relationship (LSER) fitted by multiple linear regression (Ab Rani et al., 2011; Florindo et al., 2018; Gilbert et al., 2019). It was observed that the KL solubility has a good positive correlation with the values of α and π * (Table 1 and Fig. 2). However, although DESs had a high β value, the correlation with the β value is not good. It could be seen from Table 1 that the correlation between KL solubility of LA-based DESs at 70 °C and the K-T parameters follows the equation lnS= -30.44 + 24.79α and lnS= -29.28 + 30.30π*. From the above experimental results and discussions, we could deduce that the DESs with relative higher values of α and π * generally show better performance on lignin dissolution. This is because, the high α values of DESs were key factor that correlate with the lignin extraction and dissolution efficiency during biomass pretreatment. DESs with a high α value could easily donate H-bonds to release H⁺, hence a higher degree of lignin dissolution (Lee et al., 2021; van Osch et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2018). Although there was literature showing that both high α and β of DESs were effective for lignin extraction, however, in this paper, there was no linear correlation between lignin solubility and β value (Lee et al., 2021; van Osch et al., 2017). Moreover, the values of α and π * could be an indicator for DESs to dissolve lignin. Besides the ability to donate H-bonds and the polarizability, the viscosity of the DESs in- fluences the lignin dissolution, and lower viscosity benefits KL dissolution.

In addition, the DESs composed by LA and ATMAC are more efficient for KL dissolution than previous reported LA-based DESs (Table S5) (Francisco et al., 2012; Lynam et al., 2017). For example, the KL solubility in LA-ATMAC-2:1 could reach 20.7 wt% at 60 °C (Table S5, entry 1) and 15.6 wt% in GA-ATMAC-2:1 (Table S5, entry 3). In comparison, the solubilities of KL in LA-histidine-9:1 is only 11.88 wt% at 60 °C (Table S5, entry 9) (Francisco et al., 2012). Moreover, the highest solubility of KL in LA-based DESs reported by Lynam et al. is only 13 wt% (Table S5, entries 10–12) (Lynam et al., 2017). These results confirm the good ability of LA-ATMAC-2:1 to dissolve KL.

3.3. *Characterization of the original and regenerated KL* The dissolved KL could be easily regenerated from LA-ATMAC-2:1 using water as anti-solvent. To determine the potential structure changes, the original and regenerated KL were characterized by ¹H NMR spectra, 2D HSQC NMR spectra, FT-IR spectra, SEM, and TGA.

¹H NMR spectra were firstly employed to examine the chemical structure of original KL and the regenerated one (Fig. 3). Compared with the spectra of original KL, a new sharp peak, corresponding to the Hβ of resinol substructures, (An et al., 2015) appears at 3.05 ppm in the ¹H NMR spectra of the regenerated KL, which indicates the formation of resinol substructures with the β-β' linkage via recondensation reactions. Meanwhile, another two new peaks at 6.1 and 5.6 ppm are observed,

which are assigned to Hα of β-O-4 and β-5 structure (Rashid et al., 2016). These results clearly confirm that the chemical structure of KL has been changed during dissolution and regeneration. Moreover, after the dis- solved KL was regenerated, the weak peak at 9.44 ppm disappeared (Fig. 3B), suggesting that chemical reactions in active formyl group occurred, which is consistent with the reported results (An et al., 2015). In addition, although there are some differences for the signals of methoxyl groups (intense peak at 3.79–4.07 ppm) between the original KL and the regenerated one, the changes in the methoxyl contents could not be accurately assessed owing to the signal (3.3 ppm) of residual water in DMSO-d6 and the used KL (An et al., 2015).

2D NMR is a very useful technique to analyze the structure of lignin (Mansfield et al., 2012). The 2D HSQC NMR spectra of the original KL and the regenerated one are subsequently provided in Fig. 4. The signals in 2D HSQC NMR spectra are assigned based on the previous results (Balakshin et al., 2003; Fernández-Costas et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2008; Wen et al., 2014). The detail peak assignments and the main sub-structures in KL are provided in Table S6 and Fig. 4E, respectively. First, the aliphatic region showed different linkages in KL (Fig. 4 A and 4 C), including β-O-4', β-5', and β-β', etc. The intense signal at 55.2/3.71 ppm, attributed to methoxyl groups, are observed in spectra of original KL and the regenerated one. The signals at 70.8/4.75, 84.3/4.25 and 59.9/3.38, 3.57 ppm represent the C-H correlations at the α, β, and γ positions of the β-O-4' linkage (A), respectively. By comparing the spectra in Fig. 4 A and 4 C, it is obvious that the content of β-O-4' structure (α-γ) decreases after dissolution and regeneration. Moreover, a new signal at 51.6/3.02 ppm (Bβ) is observed in the spectra of the regenerated KL (Fig. 4 C), indicating the breakage of the Bα bond after the KL was dissolved and re-generated. This result is consistent with the appearance of new peak at 1734 cm⁻¹ in FT-IR spectra (Fig. S4). The presence of Bα (at 84.3/4.59 ppm) and Bγ (at 70.5/3.73, 3.96 ppm) in the original KL and Bα, Bβ and Bγ in the generated KL represents the resinol substructures (B). The signals at 86.2/5.45 ppm (Cα-Hα), 51.3/3.64 ppm (Cβ-Hβ) and 62.8/3.67 ppm (Cγ-Hγ) confirm the existence of phenylcoumaran sub-structures (C) in both KL. The content of β-O-4' aryl ether in the original KL is 65.20/100Ar, while it drops sharply to 11.70/100Ar in regener-ated KL (Figs. 4B and 4D). It implies that the dissolution and regenera-tion of KL from the DES (LA-ATMAC-2:1) system caused the reduction of β-O-4' content. Meanwhile, the contents of other carbon-carbon bonds (such as β-5' and β-β') are reduced after being regenerated (Figs. 4B and 4D). As shown in Figs. 4B and 4D, the chemical shift of the guaiac-based unit changed from 6.69 to 6.97 ppm to 6.73-6.99 ppm after being re-generated, which is caused by the increase of the electron cloud density in the guaiac-based unit and the occurrence of a condensation reaction to generate new carbon-carbon bonds (Shen et al., 2019).

The surface structure of original KL and the regenerated one were characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM). As shown in Fig. S2, the surface structure of the original KL was relatively uniform and smooth, while the regenerated KL was rougher, indicating that the physical structure of lignin changed during the dissolution and regen- eration. Moreover, the molecular weight (Mw and Mn) significantly reduced after regeneration measured by gel permeation chromatog- raphy (Table 2), implying that the regenerated KL was dissociated or depolymerized in comparison with the original KL. Meanwhile, poly- dispersity index (Mw/Mn) of regenerated KL decreased, indicating that the dispersion of the KL became better. Additionally, in TG experiments (Fig. S3), the weight of both KLs decreased rapidly at the temperature range of 180–400 °C because the cleavage of ether bonds and the evaporation of monomeric phenols (Faravelli et al., 2010). More importantly, the decomposition temperature for the regenerated KL was lower than that of the original KL. Meanwhile, the regenerated KL provided less residual (37.32 wt%) than the original KL (54.85 wt%), suggesting that the regenerated KL occurred chemical changes in the process of dissolution and regeneration. 3.5. Mechanism of KL dissolution and biomass pretreatment in the DESs The dissolution of KL in the DESs could be explained from three as-pects, including the solubility of KL, the K-T parameters of DESs, and the structural changes of regenerated KL. The functional groups in the HBAs and HBDs have significant effect on the dissolution of KL in DESs. The -COOH groups in LA and GA could provide active protons, which enhance the H-bonds strength and enable the cleavage of various chemical bonds in lignin (Zhou et al., 2022). However, the excess -COOH groups in HBDs (e.g., MA) could form more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, resulting in higher viscosity of DESs, which reduced the mass transfer rate of the solvent system. Hence, additional energy was required to loosen the bonded structures to initiate in-teractions with lignin. Furthermore, the presence of an extensive H-bonds network weakened the ability of HBAs to compete with intra-molecular bonding in lignin, thus resulting in lower solubility of lignin. Moreover, for the DESs with the same HBD, the solubility of KL changed with the functional groups of the HBAs following the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl, which was consistent with the previously reported results (Liu et al., 2019b). The KL solubility showed good positive correlation with

the values of the K-T parameters of the prepared DESs (α and π *). DESs with a high α value could easily donate H-bonds to release H$^+$, hence a higher degree of lignin dissolution, suggesting that the dissolution of KL was mainly affected by the HBDs of the obtained DESs (Lee et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2019). As characterized by ¹H NMR, 2D HSQC NMR and FT-IR spectra, the dissolution and regeneration process involved the breaking of β-O-4, β-5 and β-β linkages, the main mechanism is as follows: DES provides active protons, and lignin is acylated in DES and positive protons are formed at Cα. The deprotonation and protonation processes are followed by the formation of a resonant stable positive charge, followed by dehydration and further fracture of the ether bond (Fig. 6), (Chen et al., 2020a; Xia et al., 2018) indicating that chemical reactions occurred when the KL was dissolved in DESs. Meanwhile, the decreased molecular weight and the lower decomposition temperature for the regenerated KL implied that the KL partially degraded during the dissolution process. Similarly, the -COOH groups in DESs could provide active protons during pretreatment of biomass. These active protons facilitate the proton-catalyzed cleavage of lignin-carbohydrate complexes (LCCs) and various chemical bonds (e.g., ether and carbon-carbon bonds) in lignin.

## 4. Conclusions In summary, DESs composed by carboxylic acid (i.e., LA, MA, and GA) as the HBD and quaternary ammonium salt (i.e., ATMAC, ChCl, TMAC, and TEAC) as the HBA, were designed for the dissolution of KL and pretreatment of poplar and pine. This study confirmed that the ability of DESs for KL dissolution is significantly affected by the chemical structure of HBDs and HBAs. The -COOH groups in HBDs could provide active protons, which enhance the H-bonds strength and enable the cleavage of various chemical bonds in lignin. However, the excess -COOH groups in HBDs could form more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, resulting in higher viscosity of DESs and reduced the lignin dissolution and extraction during biomass pretreatment. Meanwhile, the functional group in the HBA affected the solubility of KL in DESs, following the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl group. The synergistic effect of LA and ATMAC afforded LA-ATMAC-2:1 the best developed DES in this work on KL dissolution (solubility of 22.5 wt% at 70 °C) and lignocellulose delignification. Moreover, the solubility of KL shows good positive correlation with the K-T parameters α and π* of the developed DESs, while the correlation between KL solubility and β was poor. In addition, the content of β-O-4 linkages decreased after the KL was regenerated, indicating that DES achieved dissolution and extraction by breaking ether bonds during dissolution and pretreatment. DESs are a promising class of functional solvents to pretreat and dissolve lignin and even lignocellulosic biomass, and novel DES with high efficiency to pretreat biomass can be designed by the incorporating of proper HBDs and HBAs.

To both explore the most efficient DESs for ligno-cellulose dissolution and pretreatment as well as unveil the process mechanism, DESs composed by carboxylic acids as the hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and quaternary ammonium salts as the hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) were prepared and further applied for kraft lignin (KL) dissolution as well as poplar and pine pretreat-ment. We found DES composed by lactic acid (LA) and allyltrimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC) with mole ratio of 2:1 is high-efficient for the dissolution of KL. In addition, 70% poplar lignin and 82% pine lignin could be removed at 120 °C for 6 h with a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:10. Furthermore, the -OH and -COOH groups in HBDs = of DESs provided active protons to cleave ether bonds and part of carbon-carbon bonds during lignin disso-lution and extraction. Additionally, the KL solubility and the Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters (a and π * ) of the DESs showed good positive correlation. These findings give a deep insight into the dissolution mechanism of KL and pretreatment of lignocellulose, which is helpful for designing robust DESs for dissolution and pretreatment of lignocellulose. 1. Introduction Lignin is the most abundant aromatic biopolymer in nature. Meanwhile, it is a sustainable precursor for producing aromatic chemicals. In the past decades, transformation of lignin into functional materials and value-added chemicals has drawn numerous attentions. Generally, dissolution is a prerequisite for effectively utilization/conversion of lignin (Chen et al., 2020b; Ragauskas Arthur et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017a, 2017b). However, lignin is composed by the cross link of three phenylpropane structure units through diverse linkages, which makes the dissolution of lignin highly difficult (Hong et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017). Until now, several types of solvent systems have been applied in the dissolution of lignin, for example, ionic liquids (ILs), (An et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2019b; Rashid et al., 2016) mixture of ILs and water, (Xu et al., 2017) mixture of water and organic solvents (Zhang et al., 2017a, 2017b) or γ-valerolactone (Xue et al., 2016), and liquid ammonia (Strassberger et al., 2015). Although these solvent systems could dissolve lignin, they have some obvious drawbacks. Organic solvents are volatile, while liquid ammonia requires high pressure and low * Corresponding authors. Mu). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indcrop.2022.115049 Received 27 January 2022; Received in revised form 25 March 2022; Accepted 3 May 2022 Available online 9 May 2022 0926-6690/© 2022 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. temperature (Strassberger et al., 2015). ILs are usually expensive and viscous (Cao et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017a, 2017b). It is still a chal- lenge for designing novel and robust solvent systems to dissolve lignin. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are cheap, easy to prepare, and can be designed to be non-toxic, biocompatible and biodegradable (Abbott et al., 2004, 2003; Paiva et al., 2014; van Osch et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2021). Recently, applications of DESs in pretreatment of lignocellulose have gained significant attention (Francisco et al., 2012; Lou and Zhang, 2022; Wang and Lee, 2021; Xu et al., 2021). Reports have shown that organic acids based DESs are highly efficient for lignocellulose pretreatment (Tan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Fran- cisco et al., 2012). For example, Alvarez-Vasco et al. used DESs composed by organic carboxylic acid (i.e., acetic acid, levulinic acid, and lactic acid (LA)) and choline chloride for delignification of hardwood and softwoods, and LA based DES showed the highest lignin extraction yields (78.5% from hardwoods and 58.2% from softwoods) (Alvar- ez-Vasco et al., 2016). Lynam et al. found that LA-based DESs could dissolve alkali lignin with the highest solubility of 13 wt% (Lynam et al., 2017). Hong et al. reported that LA and choline chloride-based DES is more efficient on separating alkali lignin from poplar than oxalic acid H. Yu et al. Industrial Crops & Products 184 (2022) 115049 and choline chloride-based DES (Hong et al., 2020a). Liang et al. used LA-based DESs for pretreatment of corn stover and found that both alkyl chain length and functional groups of HBAs significantly influence the efficiency of pretreatment (Liang et al., 2021). These discussions indi- cated that carboxylic-based DESs (especially LA) are efficient for lignocellulose pretreatment and dissolution because of the unique mo- lecular structure of LA, in which there are simultaneously one carboxyl group and one hydroxyl group. However, the solubility of lignin in the currently developed LA-based DESs was not satisfactory, and the mechanism of the better performance of LA-based DESs has not been well unveiled. To enhance the solubility of lignin in LA-based DESs and reveal the enhancing effect of LA on lignin dissolution, herein, several carboxylic acids (i.e., LA, malic acid (MA) and glycolic acid (GA)) and quaternary ammonium salts (allyltrimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC), choline chloride (ChCl), tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC), and tetrae- thylammonium chloride (TEAC)) based DESs were prepared (Fig. S1). The solubility of kraft lignin (KL) in these DESs at 50 °C, 60 °C and 70 °C were measured. The relationship between lignin solubility and the Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters of the DESs was analyzed. The structural changes between the original and the regenerated lignin were charac- terized. In addition, pretreatment of poplar and pine with the designed DESs was conducted and the enhanced effect of the LA-based DESs on KL dissolution and lignocellulose pretreatment was investigated. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Kraft lignin (KL, with low sulfonate content) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Poplar (5 years old) wood was obtained from Hebei Province and pine (Pinus yunnanensis, 6 years old) wood was obtained from Yunnan Province. Choline chloride (ChCl), lactic acid (LA), allyl-trimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC), and glycolic acid (GA) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Malic acid (MA) and tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC) were bought from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd (Beijing, China). Tetraethylammonium chloride (TEAC) was purchased from Energy Chemical (Beijing, China). ## 2.2. Preparation of DESs The DESs were prepared by mixing the HBDs and HBAs at a molar ratio of 1:1 or 2:1 in a glass vial. Subsequently, the mixture was heated to 70 °C with a mechanical stirrer at 500 rpm until a transparent liquid was obtained. Finally, all DESs were stored under vacuum at 60 °C for 24 h to remove the contaminated trace water. 2.3. Determination of KL solubility in the prepared DESs The solubility of KL was measured based on our previously reported route (Yu et al., 2020). The KL solubility measurement consisted of a total of two steps. The first step was roughly measured, and 30 mg of KL was added to ca.1 g DES each time, and the addition is repeated until the added KL could not be completely dissolved within 1 h. The second step was accurately measured. 90% amount of the first-step achieved KL solubility was added to ca.1 g DES, then 3 mg of KL was added to DES each time until the KL could not be dissolved in 1 h. The detailed information was presented in Supplementary Information section. 2.4. *Pretreatment with DESs and composition analysis* The poplar and pine particles of sizes between 40 and 60 mesh were obtained by smash and then sieve the poplar and pine sample. After that, the wood powder was extracted with toluene–ethanol (2:1, v/v) in a Soxhlet instrument for 6 h. The poplar/pine powder were mixed with LA-ATMAC-2:1 or LA-ChCl-2:1 with a mass ratio of 1:10 and put in an oil bath at 120 °C for 6 h, and followed by dilution with ethanol. The solid components were further separated and washed with ethanol and deionized water until the filtrate clarifies, and then freeze-dried for the followed analysis. The detailed pretreatment process was given in Supplementary Information section. The chemical compositions of poplar sample and the solid substrates were determined according to a reported procedure (Sluiter et al., 2010). The content of acid-insoluble lignin (AIL, Klason lignin) was determined by measuring the weight of the residue after drying. The absorbance of acid-soluble lignin (ASL) at 240 nm was determined by UV2310-vis spectrophotometer. The deter- mination of monomeric sugars in the aqueous soluble fraction per- formed on HPAEC system (Dionex ICS 3000, USA) equipped with a Carbopac TM PA-20 column (3 mm × 150 mm, Dionex, Sunnyvale, USA) and an amperometric detector. The details could be seen in Supple- mentary Information section too. ## 2.5. Structural characterization of KL Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were performed on a Bruker Avance 400 MHz spectrometer. The weight-average (M_w) and number-average (M_n) molecular weights of the two acetylated KL samples were analyzed by Gel Permeation Chromatography (GPC, Agilent 1200). Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) analysis was conducted on a Hitachi S-4800 Scanning Electron Microscope operated at 15 kV. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) experiment was conducted on a TGA Q500 (TA Instrument Company, America). Fourier Transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra were recorded on a Prestige-21 FT-IR Spectroscopy (Shimadzu, Japan). Detailed information was given in Supplementary Information section. 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Dissolution of KL in DESs The prepared DESs (Table S1) were denoted as HBD-HBA-x, where x represents the molar ratio of HBD and HBA. In Table S1, LA-TMAC-1:1 and GA-TMAC-1:1 could not form DESs. Subsequently, the prepared DESs were applied to dissolve KL at different temperatures (Fig. 1). Fig. 1 shows that the solubility of KL in all examined DESs increases with the dissolution temperature. When the molar ratio of HBD and HBA was 1:1, at 50 °C, LA-ATMAC-1:1 and LA-ChCl-1:1 could dissolve KL, but the solubility of KL in LA-TEMC-1:1 is less than 1 wt%. As shown in Fig. 1, LA-ATMAC-1:1 provides the best lignin solubility of 15.6 wt% at 70 °C, while the lignin solubility is only 2.9 wt% in LA-TEMC-1:1 at 70 °C. Fig. 1B shows that the solubility of KL is significantly enhanced to 22.5 wt% when the molar ratio of HBD and HBA increase to 2:1 for LA-ATMAC-2:1 at 70 °C. Notably, the solubility of KL at 70 °C increases with the following order: LA-TEAC-2:1 < LA-TMAC-2:1 < LA-ChCl-2:1 < LA-ATMAC-2:1. For the GA-based DESs, a similar tendency was observed (Fig. 1C and D). The GA-ATMAC-x showed the best performance at the same GA/HBA molar ratio, and high molar ratio of GA and HBAs is beneficial for the dissolution of KL. Meanwhile, the solubility of KL at 70 °C increases with the following order: GA-TEAC-2:1 < GA-TMAC-2:1 < GA-ChCl-2:1 < GA-ATMAC-2:1. GA-ATMAC-2:1 shows the maximum KL solubility of 19.1 wt% at 70 °C among all GA-based DESs (Fig. 1). Table S2 indicates that all the prepared MA-based DESs show poor performance on the KL dissolution even at 70 °C. From the above results, the functional groups in the employed HBAs significantly affect the KL dissolution, which followed the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl, and meanwhile, the KL solubility decreases with the increase of the cation size in HBAs, e.g., LA-TEAC-2:1 < LA-TMAC-2:1 and GA-TEAC-2:1 < GA-TMAC-2:1. Besides, for the DESs with same HBA, LA and GA-based DESs show better performance on KL dissolution at all determined temperatures (i. e., 50 °C, 60 °C and 70 °C) (Fig. 1), while the solubility of KL in MA- 2 H. From the chemical structure of the used HBDs (LA, MA, and GA), the main difference of the used HBDs lies in that there are two -COOH groups in MA, while only one -COOH group in both LA and GA. Meanwhile, all the three HBDs contain one -OH group. The -OH group and -COOH groups in the HBD are beneficial for lignin dissolution, but more than one -COOH groups weaken the lignin dissolution (Tan et al., 2019). Consistent with Francisco's results (Francisco et al., 2012), MA-based DESs show poor KL dissolution ability. The presence of two -COOH groups in MA increases the number of hydrogen bonds and extensive dimer chains, which significantly increase the viscosity (Table S3) and thus decrease mass transfer and KL dissolution. In comparison, GA- and LA-based DESs perform similarly on KL dissolution, and the solubility of KL in these two types of DESs vary with the type of HBA and the HBD/HBA molar ratio. For example, the lignin solubility in LA-TMAC-2:1 is higher than that in GA-TMAC-2:1, while GA-TEAC-2:1 shows higher solubility than LA-TEAC-2:1. Moreover, LA-ChCl-1:1 shows higher KL solubility than GA-ChCl-1:1, but the solubility of KL in LA-ChCl-2:1 is lower than that in GA-ChCl-2:1. The different performance of the prepared LA- and GA-based DESs to dissolve KL will be discussed in the following section. 3.2. The effect of DESs' K-T parameters on KL dissolution K-T empirical parameters (i.e., α, β, and π *) of the solvents could be employed to evaluate the ability of the solvents to dissolve lignocellu-lose components. These parameters can be applied to quantify hydrogen-bond donating ability (acidity, α), hydrogen-bond accepting ability (basicity, β) and the polarizability (π*) of the solvents. The K-T empirical parameters of the prepared LA- and GA-based DESs were determined and given in Table S4. The correlation between KL solubil-ities (Fig. 1) and the K-T parameters Table S4 is very poor if all the LA-and GA-based DESs are considered. However, after carefully analyzing the obtained results, some regularities could still be observed. First, the solubilities of KL in LA- and GA-based DESs are similar when they have the same HBA and molar ratio of HBD/HBA (Fig. 1). Correspondingly, K-T empirical parameters of LA- and GA-based DESS with same HBA and molar ratio of HBD/HBA are similar (Table S4) although the correlation between KL solubility and the K-T parameters is not completely consistent. Second, compared with other HBAs, the alkyl chain of TEMC is longer and its volume is larger than that of the other three HBAs, which leads to its larger steric hindrance, causing the HBDs has a weak ability to form H-bonds with it (Zhou et al., 2022). In addition, the molar ratio of HBAs and HBDs also affects the dissolution ability of lignin. When the molar ratio of HBDs increased, LA and GA could provide more active protons, which promoted the dissolution of lignin (Zhou et al., 2022). As a result, LA-TEAC-1:1 and GA-TEAC-1:1 show the lowest values of α and π*, indicating that they have the poorest hydrogen-bond donating ability and lowest polarity. In contrast, the solvents possessing stronger hydrogen-bond donating ability and higher polarity have better ability to dissolve lignin (Liu et al., 2019a). Thereby, the solubility of KL in LA-TEAC-1:1 and GA-TEAC-1:1 is very low. From the above experimental results and discussions, we could deduce that the DESs with relative higher values of α and π * generally show better performance on lignin dissolution. This is because, the high α values of DESs were key factor that correlate with the lignin extraction and dissolution efficiency during biomass pretreatment. DESs with a high α value could easily donate H-bonds to release H⁺, hence a higher degree of lignin dissolution (Lee et al., 2021; van Osch et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2018). Although there was literature showing that both high α and β of DESs were effective for lignin extraction, however, in this paper, there was no linear correlation between lignin solubility and β value (Lee et al., 2021; van Osch et al., 2017). Moreover, the values of α and π * could be an indicator for DESs to dissolve lignin. Besides the ability to donate H-bonds and the polarizability, the viscosity of the DESs in- fluences the lignin dissolution, and lower viscosity benefits KL dissolution. In addition, the DESs composed by LA and ATMAC are more efficient for KL dissolution than previous reported LA-based DESs (Table S5) (Francisco et al., 2012; Lynam et al., 2017). For example, the KL solubility in LA-ATMAC-2:1 could reach 20.7 wt% at 60 °C (Table S5, entry 1) and 15.6 wt% in GA-ATMAC-2:1 (Table S5, entry 3). Moreover, the highest solubility of KL in LA-based DESs reported by Lynam et al. is only 13 wt% (Table S5, entries 10–12) (Lynam et al., 2017). These results confirm the good ability of LA-ATMAC-2:1 to dissolve KL. 3.3. *Characterization of the original and regenerated KL* The dissolved KL could be easily regenerated from LA-ATMAC-2:1 using water as anti-solvent. To determine the potential structure changes, the original and regenerated KL were characterized by ¹H NMR spectra, 2D HSQC NMR spectra, FT-IR spectra, SEM, and TGA. ¹H NMR spectra were firstly employed to examine the chemical structure of original KL and the regenerated one (Fig. 3). Compared with the spectra of original KL, a new sharp peak, corresponding to the Hβ of resinol substructures, (An et al., 2015) appears at 3.05 ppm in the ¹H NMR spectra of the regenerated KL, which indicates the formation of resinol substructures with the β-β' linkage via recondensation reactions. Meanwhile, another two new peaks at 6.1 and 5.6 ppm are observed, which are assigned to Hα of β-O-4 and β-5 structure (Rashid et al., 2016). These results clearly confirm that the chemical structure of KL has been changed during dissolution and regeneration. Moreover, after the dis- solved KL was regenerated, the weak peak at 9.44 ppm disappeared (Fig. 3B), suggesting that chemical reactions in active formyl group occurred, which is consistent with the reported results (An et al., 2015). In addition, although there are some differences for the signals of methoxyl groups (intense peak at 3.79–4.07 ppm) between the original KL and the regenerated one, the changes in the methoxyl contents could not be accurately assessed owing to the signal (3.3 ppm) of residual water in DMSO-d6 and the used KL (An et al., 2015). 2D NMR is a very useful technique to analyze the structure of lignin (Mansfield et al., 2012). The 2D HSQC NMR spectra of the original KL and the regenerated one are subsequently provided in Fig. 4. The signals in 2D HSQC NMR spectra are assigned based on the previous results (Balakshin et al., 2003; Fernández-Costas et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2008; Wen et al., 2014). The detail peak assignments and the main sub-structures in KL are provided in Table S6 and Fig. 4E, respectively. First, the aliphatic region showed different linkages in KL (Fig. 4 A and 4 C), including β-O-4', β-5', and β-β', etc. The intense signal at 55.2/3.71 ppm, attributed to methoxyl groups, are observed in spectra of original KL and the regenerated one. The signals at 70.8/4.75, 84.3/4.25 and 59.9/3.38, 3.57 ppm represent the C-H correlations at the α, β, and γ positions of the β-O-4' linkage (A), respectively. By comparing the spectra in Fig. 4 A and 4 C, it is obvious that the content of β-O-4' structure (α-γ) decreases after dissolution and regeneration. Moreover, a new signal at 51.6/3.02 ppm (Bβ) is observed in the spectra of the regenerated KL (Fig. 4 C), indicating the breakage of the Bα bond after the KL was dissolved and re-generated. This result is consistent with the appearance of new peak at 1734 cm⁻¹ in FT-IR spectra (Fig. S4). The presence of Bα (at 84.3/4.59 ppm) and Bγ (at 70.5/3.73, 3.96 ppm) in the original KL and Bα, Bβ and Bγ in the generated KL represents the resinol substructures (B). The signals at 86.2/5.45 ppm (Cα-Hα), 51.3/3.64 ppm (Cβ-Hβ) and 62.8/3.67 ppm (Cγ-Hγ) confirm the existence of phenylcoumaran sub-structures (C) in both KL. The content of β-O-4' aryl ether in the original KL is 65.20/100Ar, while it drops sharply to 11.70/100Ar in regener-ated KL (Figs. 4B and 4D). It implies that the dissolution and regenera-tion of KL from the DES (LA-ATMAC-2:1) system caused the reduction of β-O-4' content. Meanwhile, the contents of other carbon-carbon bonds (such as β-5' and β-β') are reduced after being regenerated (Figs. 4B and 4D). As shown in Figs. 4B and 4D, the chemical shift of the guaiac-based unit changed from 6.69 to 6.97 ppm to 6.73-6.99 ppm after being re-generated, which is caused by the increase of the electron cloud density in the guaiac-based unit and the occurrence of a condensation reaction to generate new carbon-carbon bonds (Shen et al., 2019). The surface structure of original KL and the regenerated one were characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM). As shown in Fig. S2, the surface structure of the original KL was relatively uniform and smooth, while the regenerated KL was rougher, indicating that the physical structure of lignin changed during the dissolution and regen- eration. Meanwhile, the regenerated KL provided less residual (37.32 wt%) than the original KL (54.85 wt%), suggesting that the regenerated KL occurred chemical changes in the process of dissolution and regeneration. Mechanism of KL dissolution and biomass pretreatment in the DESs The dissolution of KL in the DESs could be explained from three as-pects, including the solubility of KL, the K-T parameters of DESs, and the structural changes of regenerated KL. The functional groups in the HBAs and HBDs have significant effect on the dissolution of KL in DESs. The -COOH groups in LA and GA could provide active protons, which enhance the H-bonds strength and enable the cleavage of various chemical bonds in lignin (Zhou et al., 2022). However, the excess -COOH groups in HBDs (e.g., MA) could form more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, resulting in higher viscosity of DESs, which reduced the mass transfer rate of the solvent system. Hence, additional energy was required to loosen the bonded structures to initiate in-teractions with lignin. Furthermore, the presence of an extensive H-bonds network weakened the ability of HBAs to compete with intra-molecular bonding in lignin, thus resulting in lower solubility of lignin. Moreover, for the DESs with the same HBD, the solubility of KL changed with the functional groups of the HBAs following the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl, which was consistent with the previously reported results (Liu et al., 2019b). The KL solubility showed good positive correlation with the values of the K-T parameters of the prepared DESs (α and π *). DESs with a high α value could easily donate H-bonds to release H$^+$, hence a higher degree of lignin dissolution, suggesting that the dissolution of KL was mainly affected by the HBDs of the obtained DESs (Lee et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2019). As characterized by ¹H NMR, 2D HSQC NMR and FT-IR spectra, the dissolution and regeneration process involved the breaking of β-O-4, β-5 and β-β linkages, the main mechanism is as follows: DES provides active protons, and lignin is acylated in DES and positive protons are formed at Cα. The deprotonation and protonation processes are followed by the formation of a resonant stable positive charge, followed by dehydration and further fracture of the ether bond (Fig. 6), (Chen et al., 2020a; Xia et al., 2018) indicating that chemical reactions occurred when the KL was dissolved in DESs. Meanwhile, the decreased molecular weight and the lower decomposition temperature for the regenerated KL implied that the KL partially degraded during the dissolution process. Similarly, the -COOH groups in DESs could provide active protons during pretreatment of biomass. These active protons facilitate the proton-catalyzed cleavage of lignin-carbohydrate complexes (LCCs) and various chemical bonds (e.g., ether and carbon-carbon bonds) in lignin. ## 4. Conclusions In summary, DESs composed by carboxylic acid (i.e., LA, MA, and GA) as the HBD and quaternary ammonium salt (i.e., ATMAC, ChCl, TMAC, and TEAC) as the HBA, were designed for the dissolution of KL and pretreatment of poplar and pine. This study confirmed that the ability of DESs for KL dissolution is significantly affected by the chemical structure of HBDs and HBAs. The -COOH groups in HBDs could provide active protons, which enhance the H-bonds strength and enable the cleavage of various chemical bonds in lignin. However, the excess -COOH groups in HBDs could form more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, resulting in higher viscosity of DESs and reduced the lignin dissolution and extraction during biomass pretreatment. Meanwhile, the functional group in the HBA affected the solubility of KL in DESs, following the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl group. The synergistic effect of LA and ATMAC afforded LA-ATMAC-2:1 the best developed DES in this work on KL dissolution (solubility of 22.5 wt% at 70 °C) and lignocellulose delignification. Moreover, the solubility of KL shows good positive correlation with the K-T parameters α and π* of the developed DESs, while the correlation between KL solubility and β was poor. In addition, the content of β-O-4 linkages decreased after the KL was regenerated, indicating that DES achieved dissolution and extraction by breaking ether bonds during dissolution and pretreatment. DESs are a promising class of functional solvents to pretreat and dissolve lignin and even lignocellulosic biomass, and novel DES with high efficiency to pretreat biomass can be designed by the incorporating of proper HBDs and HBAs. Introduction Lignin is the most abundant aromatic biopolymer in nature. Meanwhile, it is a sustainable precursor for producing aromatic chemicals. In the past decades, transformation of lignin into functional materials and value-added chemicals has drawn numerous attentions. Generally, dissolution is a prerequisite for effectively utilization/conversion of lignin (Chen et al., 2020b; Ragauskas Arthur et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017a, 2017b). However, lignin is composed by the cross link of three phenylpropane structure units through diverse linkages, which makes the dissolution of lignin highly difficult (Hong et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017). Until now, several types of solvent systems have been applied in the dissolution of lignin, for example, ionic liquids (ILs), (An et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2019b; Rashid et al., 2016) mixture of ILs and water, (Xu et al., 2017) mixture of water and organic solvents (Zhang et al., 2017a, 2017b) or γ-valerolactone (Xue et al., 2016), and liquid ammonia (Strassberger et al., 2015). Although these solvent systems could dissolve lignin, they have some obvious drawbacks. Organic solvents are volatile, while liquid ammonia requires high pressure and low * Corresponding authors. It is still a chal- lenge for designing novel and robust solvent systems to dissolve lignin. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are cheap, easy to prepare, and can be designed to be non-toxic, biocompatible and biodegradable (Abbott et al., 2004, 2003; Paiva et al., 2014; van Osch et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2021). Recently, applications of DESs in pretreatment of lignocellulose have gained significant attention (Francisco et al., 2012; Lou and Zhang, 2022; Wang and Lee, 2021; Xu et al., 2021). Reports have shown that organic acids based DESs are highly efficient for lignocellulose pretreatment (Tan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Fran- cisco et al., 2012). For example, Alvarez-Vasco et al. used DESs composed by organic carboxylic acid (i.e., acetic acid, levulinic acid, and lactic acid (LA)) and choline chloride for delignification of hardwood and softwoods, and LA based DES showed the highest lignin extraction yields (78.5% from hardwoods and 58.2% from softwoods) (Alvar- ez-Vasco et al., 2016). Lynam et al. found that LA-based DESs could dissolve alkali lignin with the highest solubility of 13 wt% (Lynam et al., 2017). Liang et al. used LA-based DESs for pretreatment of corn stover and found that both alkyl chain length and functional groups of HBAs significantly influence the efficiency of pretreatment (Liang et al., 2021). These discussions indi- cated that carboxylic-based DESs (especially LA) are efficient for lignocellulose pretreatment and dissolution because of the unique mo- lecular structure of LA, in which there are simultaneously one carboxyl group and one hydroxyl group. However, the solubility of lignin in the currently developed LA-based DESs was not satisfactory, and the mechanism of the better performance of LA-based DESs has not been well unveiled. To enhance the solubility of lignin in LA-based DESs and reveal the enhancing effect of LA on lignin dissolution, herein, several carboxylic acids (i.e., LA, malic acid (MA) and glycolic acid (GA)) and quaternary ammonium salts (allyltrimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC), choline chloride (ChCl), tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC), and tetrae- thylammonium chloride (TEAC)) based DESs were prepared (Fig. S1). The solubility of kraft lignin (KL) in these DESs at 50 °C, 60 °C and 70 °C were measured. The relationship between lignin solubility and the Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters of the DESs was analyzed. The structural changes between the original and the regenerated lignin were charac- terized. In addition, pretreatment of poplar and pine with the designed DESs was conducted and the enhanced effect of the LA-based DESs on KL dissolution and lignocellulose pretreatment was investigated. ## 2. Poplar (5 years old) wood was obtained from Hebei Province and pine (Pinus yunnanensis, 6 years old) wood was obtained from Yunnan Province. Choline chloride (ChCl), lactic acid (LA), allyl-trimethylammonium chloride (ATMAC), and glycolic acid (GA) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Malic acid (MA) and tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC) were bought from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd (Beijing, China). Tetraethylammonium chloride (TEAC) was purchased from Energy Chemical (Beijing, China). ## 2.2. Preparation of DESs The DESs were prepared by mixing the HBDs and HBAs at a molar ratio of 1:1 or 2:1 in a glass vial. Subsequently, the mixture was heated to 70 °C with a mechanical stirrer at 500 rpm until a transparent liquid was obtained. Finally, all DESs were stored under vacuum at 60 °C for 24 h to remove the contaminated trace water. 2.3. Determination of KL solubility in the prepared DESs The solubility of KL was measured based on our previously reported route (Yu et al., 2020). The KL solubility measurement consisted of a total of two steps. The first step was roughly measured, and 30 mg of KL was added to ca.1 g DES each time, and the addition is repeated until the added KL could not be completely dissolved within 1 h. The second step was accurately measured. 90% amount of the first-step achieved KL solubility was added to ca.1 g DES, then 3 mg of KL was added to DES each time until the KL could not be dissolved in 1 h. In comparison, GA- and LA-based DESs perform similarly on KL dissolution, and the solubility of KL in these two types of DESs vary with the type of HBA and the HBD/HBA molar ratio. For example, the lignin solubility in LA-TMAC-2:1 is higher than that in GA-TMAC-2:1, while GA-TEAC-2:1 shows higher solubility than LA-TEAC-2:1. Moreover, LA-ChCl-1:1 shows higher KL solubility than GA-ChCl-1:1, but the solubility of KL in LA-ChCl-2:1 is lower than that in GA-ChCl-2:1. The different performance of the prepared LA- and GA-based DESs to dissolve KL will be discussed in the following section. 3.2. The effect of DESs' K-T parameters on KL dissolution K-T empirical parameters (i.e., α, β, and π *) of the solvents could be employed to evaluate the ability of the solvents to dissolve lignocellu-lose components. These parameters can be applied to quantify hydrogen-bond donating ability (acidity, α), hydrogen-bond accepting ability (basicity, β) and the polarizability (π*) of the solvents. The K-T empirical parameters of the prepared LA- and GA-based DESs were determined and given in Table S4. The correlation between KL solubil-ities (Fig. 1) and the K-T parameters Table S4 is very poor if all the LA-and GA-based DESs are considered. However, after carefully analyzing the obtained results, some regularities could still be observed. First, the solubilities of KL in LA- and GA-based DESs are similar when they have the same HBA and molar ratio of HBD/HBA (Fig. 1). Correspondingly, K-T empirical parameters of LA- and GA-based DESS with same HBA and molar ratio of HBD/HBA are similar (Table S4) although the correlation between KL solubility and the K-T parameters is not completely consistent. Second, compared with other HBAs, the alkyl chain of TEMC is longer and its volume is larger than that of the other three HBAs, which leads to its larger steric hindrance, causing the HBDs has a weak ability to form H-bonds with it (Zhou et al., 2022). In addition, the molar ratio of HBAs and HBDs also affects the dissolution ability of lignin. When the molar ratio of HBDs increased, LA and GA could provide more active protons, which promoted the dissolution of lignin (Zhou et al., 2022). As a result, LA-TEAC-1:1 and GA-TEAC-1:1 show the lowest values of α and π*, indicating that they have the poorest hydrogen-bond donating ability and lowest polarity. In contrast, the solvents possessing stronger hydrogen-bond donating ability and higher polarity have better ability to dissolve lignin (Liu et al., 2019a). Thereby, the solubility of KL in LA-TEAC-1:1 and GA-TEAC-1:1 is very low. Besides the ability to donate H-bonds and the polarizability, the viscosity of the DESs in- fluences the lignin dissolution, and lower viscosity benefits KL dissolution. These results confirm the good ability of LA-ATMAC-2:1 to dissolve KL. 3.3. *Characterization of the original and regenerated KL* The dissolved KL could be easily regenerated from LA-ATMAC-2:1 using water as anti-solvent. To determine the potential structure changes, the original and regenerated KL were characterized by ¹H NMR spectra, 2D HSQC NMR spectra, FT-IR spectra, SEM, and TGA. ¹H NMR spectra were firstly employed to examine the chemical structure of original KL and the regenerated one (Fig. 3). Compared with the spectra of original KL, a new sharp peak, corresponding to the Hβ of resinol substructures, (An et al., 2015) appears at 3.05 ppm in the ¹H NMR spectra of the regenerated KL, which indicates the formation of resinol substructures with the β-β' linkage via recondensation reactions. Meanwhile, another two new peaks at 6.1 and 5.6 ppm are observed, which are assigned to Hα of β-O-4 and β-5 structure (Rashid et al., 2016). These results clearly confirm that the chemical structure of KL has been changed during dissolution and regeneration. Moreover, after the dis- solved KL was regenerated, the weak peak at 9.44 ppm disappeared (Fig. 3B), suggesting that chemical reactions in active formyl group occurred, which is consistent with the reported results (An et al., 2015). In addition, although there are some differences for the signals of methoxyl groups (intense peak at 3.79–4.07 ppm) between the original KL and the regenerated one, the changes in the methoxyl contents could not be accurately assessed owing to the signal (3.3 ppm) of residual water in DMSO-d6 and the used KL (An et al., 2015). 2D NMR is a very useful technique to analyze the structure of lignin (Mansfield et al., 2012). The 2D HSQC NMR spectra of the original KL and the regenerated one are subsequently provided in Fig. 4. The signals in 2D HSQC NMR spectra are assigned based on the previous results (Balakshin et al., 2003; Fernández-Costas et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2008; Wen et al., 2014). The detail peak assignments and the main sub-structures in KL are provided in Table S6 and Fig. 4E, respectively. First, the aliphatic region showed different linkages in KL (Fig. 4 A and 4 C), including β-O-4', β-5', and β-β', etc. The intense signal at 55.2/3.71 ppm, attributed to methoxyl groups, are observed in spectra of original KL and the regenerated one. The signals at 70.8/4.75, 84.3/4.25 and 59.9/3.38, 3.57 ppm represent the C-H correlations at the α, β, and γ positions of the β-O-4' linkage (A), respectively. By comparing the spectra in Fig. 4 A and 4 C, it is obvious that the content of β-O-4' structure (α-γ) decreases after dissolution and regeneration. Moreover, a new signal at 51.6/3.02 ppm (Bβ) is observed in the spectra of the regenerated KL (Fig. 4 C), indicating the breakage of the Bα bond after the KL was dissolved and re-generated. This result is consistent with the appearance of new peak at 1734 cm⁻¹ in FT-IR spectra (Fig. S4). The presence of Bα (at 84.3/4.59 ppm) and Bγ (at 70.5/3.73, 3.96 ppm) in the original KL and Bα, Bβ and Bγ in the generated KL represents the resinol substructures (B). Mechanism of KL dissolution and biomass pretreatment in the DESs The dissolution of KL in the DESs could be explained from three as-pects, including the solubility of KL, the K-T parameters of DESs, and the structural changes of regenerated KL. The functional groups in the HBAs and HBDs have significant effect on the dissolution of KL in DESs. The -COOH groups in LA and GA could provide active protons, which enhance the H-bonds strength and enable the cleavage of various chemical bonds in lignin (Zhou et al., 2022). However, the excess -COOH groups in HBDs (e.g., MA) could form more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, resulting in higher viscosity of DESs, which reduced the mass transfer rate of the solvent system. Hence, additional energy was required to loosen the bonded structures to initiate in-teractions with lignin. Furthermore, the presence of an extensive H-bonds network weakened the ability of HBAs to compete with intra-molecular bonding in lignin, thus resulting in lower solubility of lignin. Moreover, for the DESs with the same HBD, the solubility of KL changed with the functional groups of the HBAs following the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl, which was consistent with the previously reported results (Liu et al., 2019b). The KL solubility showed good positive correlation with the values of the K-T parameters of the prepared DESs (α and π *). DESs with a high α value could easily donate H-bonds to release H$^+$, hence a higher degree of lignin dissolution, suggesting that the dissolution of KL was mainly affected by the HBDs of the obtained DESs (Lee et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2019). As characterized by ¹H NMR, 2D HSQC NMR and FT-IR spectra, the dissolution and regeneration process involved the breaking of β-O-4, β-5 and β-β linkages, the main mechanism is as follows: DES provides active protons, and lignin is acylated in DES and positive protons are formed at Cα. The deprotonation and protonation processes are followed by the formation of a resonant stable positive charge, followed by dehydration and further fracture of the ether bond (Fig. 6), (Chen et al., 2020a; Xia et al., 2018) indicating that chemical reactions occurred when the KL was dissolved in DESs. Meanwhile, the decreased molecular weight and the lower decomposition temperature for the regenerated KL implied that the KL partially degraded during the dissolution process. Similarly, the -COOH groups in DESs could provide active protons during pretreatment of biomass. These active protons facilitate the proton-catalyzed cleavage of lignin-carbohydrate complexes (LCCs) and various chemical bonds (e.g., ether and carbon-carbon bonds) in lignin. ## 4. Conclusions In summary, DESs composed by carboxylic acid (i.e., LA, MA, and GA) as the HBD and quaternary ammonium salt (i.e., ATMAC, ChCl, TMAC, and TEAC) as the HBA, were designed for the dissolution of KL and pretreatment of poplar and pine. This study confirmed that the ability of DESs for KL dissolution is significantly affected by the chemical structure of HBDs and HBAs. The -COOH groups in HBDs could provide active protons, which enhance the H-bonds strength and enable the cleavage of various chemical bonds in lignin. However, the excess -COOH groups in HBDs could form more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, resulting in higher viscosity of DESs and reduced the lignin dissolution and extraction during biomass pretreatment. Meanwhile, the functional group in the HBA affected the solubility of KL in DESs, following the order: C=C > -OH > alkyl group. The synergistic effect of LA and ATMAC afforded LA-ATMAC-2:1 the best developed DES in this work on KL dissolution (solubility of 22.5 wt% at 70 °C) and lignocellulose delignification. Moreover, the solubility of KL shows good positive correlation with the K-T parameters α and π* of the developed DESs, while the correlation between KL solubility and β was poor. In addition, the content of β-O-4 linkages decreased after the KL was regenerated, indicating that DES achieved dissolution and extraction by breaking ether bonds during dissolution and pretreatment. DESs are a promising class of functional solvents to pretreat and dissolve lignin and even lignocellulosic biomass, and novel DES with high efficiency to pretreat biomass can be designed by the incorporating of proper HBDs and HBAs.
